title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted 4D Dynamic Long-Axial PET Imaging for the Detection of Early Pancreatic Cancer Lesions
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ruijin Hospital; conditions: Pancreas Carcinoma, PDAC - Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 50; status: RECRUITING] Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and early detection of pancreatic lesions is of great importance for improving patient outcomes. In this study, whole-body imaging with FDG and FAPI will be used to visualize the early development of pancreatic cancer lesions from multiple perspectives, including glucose metabolism, tumor fibrotic stroma, and integrin receptor expression. Furthermore, leveraging the advantages of four-dimensional dynamic long-axial PET imaging, artificial intelligence-assisted lesion detection and analysis will be performed to characterize lesions and differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. The imaging findings will subsequently be compared with postoperative histopathological results to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the proposed imaging approaches.

title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
desc: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?
desc: Can a large language model (LLM) write the parameters of a medical image classifier from medical knowledge alone, without any training data? Such classifiers normally require labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable. We investigate this question through weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM writes or adapts the weights and biases of a neural network directly, without optimisation on training data. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra each generate the parameters of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use and without access to any image. We compare these networks against zero-shot MedSigLIP and against the same architecture trained on labels using the Adam optimiser, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities: chest X-ray, breast ultrasound and abdominal CT (all from MedMNIST), and pelvic MRI (SynthUterus). The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with a mean test AUC of 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both models outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. However, the same network trained with Adam on only 256 labelled images achieves a higher AUC on every MedMNIST task (mean AUC 0.828). On SynthUterus, Opus attains an AUC of 0.764, whereas Astra falls below chance (AUC 0.136) owing to a systematic error. These results show that LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but that they do not yet replace training data. We release the protocol, logs and all generated weights at https://github.com/MaximilianLindholz/weight-space-programming-medical.

title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
desc: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To overcome these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients, we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves preprocessing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
desc: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.

Weakly supervised deep learning predicts perineural invasion from H&E whole-slide images in tongue squamous cell carcinoma: development and external validation.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Perineural invasion (PNI) in tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) is associated with aggressive behavior and poor outcomes, yet it can be under-recognized on H&E sections because it is often focal and interpretation varies. Manual assessment of PNI suffers from significant interobserver variability, motivating AI-based decision support. We developed and externally validated a weakly supervised WSI model to predict PNI in TSCC. We retrospectively analyzed 1,511 digitized H&E whole-slide images from 629 patients at two centers. Patient-level partitioning yielded an internal training cohort of 305 patients and 787 WSIs, an internal validation cohort of 132 patients and 340 WSIs, and an external test cohort of 192 patients and 384 WSIs. Non-overlapping tiling generated 41,552,500 candidate patches before tissue-background exclusion, of which 7,813,555 unique tissue patches were retained for analysis. A two-stage pipeline was used: patch-level modeling and MIL-based slide aggregation. ResNet50 was selected over Inception_v3 and SimpleViT as the feature extractor. Patch-level prediction probabilities and image features were aggregated into a 101-dimensional patch likelihood histogram (PLH) and a 101-dimensional visual bag-of-words (BoW) representation, respectively. For conventional classifiers, the two representations were concatenated into a 202-dimensional vector, followed by z-score normalization and LASSO feature selection. For the Transformer, the two representations were processed separately using PCA, independently projected into 128-dimensional embedding spaces, and integrated using four-head cross-attention. Performance was assessed by ROC, decision curve analysis (DCA), and calibration. The internal training, internal validation, and external test cohorts included 305, 132, and 192 patients, respectively. PNI prevalence was 82.3%, 79.5%, and 72.9% in these cohorts, respectively. The Transformer fusion model achieved AUCs of 0.990 in the training cohort, 0.968 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.940 in the external test cohort. Calibration and decision curve analysis were used to characterize the model's predicted probabilities and modeled net benefit in the retrospective study cohorts. Patch-level Grad-CAM was used to generate qualitative saliency visualisations associated with ResNet50 patch-level PNI scores. title: LLM-Supported Pain Neuroscience Education for Physiotherapy Students
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: İsmail Palalı; conditions: Pain, Chronic Pain, Health Professions Education; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 120; status: COMPLETED] Physiotherapists need to explain pain to patients in a way that is scientifically accurate, understandable, and non-threatening. Pain neuroscience education (PNE) improves students' pain knowledge, but it is unclear whether this translates into retained ability to explain pain to patients. This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding structured feedback from a large language model (LLM; GPT-5.2 Instant, OpenAI, via the ChatGPT interface) to a standardized four-week PNE programme improves undergraduate physiotherapy students' pain-explanation competence compared with the same programme using standardized expert-developed (non-AI) feedback. The primary outcome was Pain Explanation Competence (PEC) on a previously unseen clinical transfer scenario, assessed without AI access 12 weeks after the intervention by three assessors blinded to group allocation.

title: Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
desc: Nature Medicine, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04716-9 This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations.

title: Risk prediction models for macrovascular complications in type 2 diabetes mellitus: from traditional risk scores to multimodal intelligent prediction.
desc: [Frontiers in endocrinology] Macrovascular complications are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Early risk identification and accurate risk stratification are essential for both primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention. With the rapid development of electronic health records, medical imaging, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI), risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications have evolved from traditional statistical approaches to machine learning-, deep learning-, and multimodal AI-driven models. However, despite substantial improvements in predictive performance, current models remain limited by heterogeneous target populations, inconsistent outcome definitions, insufficient external validation, limited clinical interpretability, and inadequate real-world implementation, thereby restricting their clinical translation. This review summarizes the evolution, data sources, modeling methodologies, clinical applications, and future perspectives of risk prediction models for macrovascular complications in T2DM. We first describe the transition from conventional cardiovascular risk scores, including the Framingham Risk Score, to diabetes-specific models such as the UKPDS Risk Engine, ADVANCE, RECODe, and SCORE2-Diabetes, followed by the emergence of AI-based prediction models. We then review the major data sources used in contemporary prediction models, including clinical characteristics, laboratory biomarkers, vascular function and imaging, multi-omics profiles, and wearable device-derived data. Furthermore, we compare the strengths and limitations of traditional statistical methods, machine learning, deep learning, and multitask learning with respect to predictive performance, interpretability, and clinical applicability, and discuss the major challenges related to study design, external validation, data quality, algorithmic bias, and real-world implementation. Finally, we propose that future risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications will evolve from single-source data to multimodal data integration, from static risk estimation to dynamic risk trajectories, from single outcomes to multiple interconnected cardiovascular outcomes, from prognosis prediction to individualized treatment benefit prediction, and from standalone algorithms to continuously learning clinical decision support systems. title: Effect of AI-Assisted Hand Hygiene Training on Hand Hygiene Competency in Newly Hired Workers
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital; conditions: Healthy Adult Participants; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 260; status: COMPLETED] The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted training works better than usual training. The training aims to improve handwashing skill in newly hired healthcare workers. The AI-assisted training uses a screen that shows feedback right away. The main questions it aims to answer are: Does AI-assisted training lead to higher overall handwashing skill scores than usual training? Does AI-assisted training improve harder handwashing steps? These include interlaced fingers, locked fingers, and fingertip rubbing. Researchers will compare AI-assisted training to usual instructor-led training. They will see if AI-assisted training improves handwashing skill. Participants will: Attend a 30-minute class on the World Health Organization (WHO) seven-step handwashing method. The class also explains how the skill test works. Be assigned by chance to usual training or AI-assisted training. Both trainings last 45 minutes. In the AI-assisted group, use a camera and screen. The screen shows their hand movements and gives feedback right away. This helps them correct their movements. Take a final handwashing skill test. The same AI system scores 12 parts of the WHO seven-step method. Two hundred sixty newly hired healthcare workers joined this study at one hospital in China. They included doctors, nurses, research staff, lab staff, and support staff.

title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
desc: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
desc: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

title: Natural-language cohort queries on a hospital data platform: accuracy and provenance in a real-world evaluation
desc: Background: Accessing routinely collected clinical data for research remains technically demanding across heterogeneous hospital systems. This proof-of-concept study aimed to evaluate the accuracy and query-level traceability of a commercial natural-language (NL) data-query platform implemented at a university hospital. Methods: An on-premises data integration platform with an NL query interface (AIRE; Briya, Tel Aviv, Israel) was connected to the institutional health data platform across three tertiary-care hospitals under an approved pseudonymization and governance framework. Implementation comprised regulatory and governance approval, and IT deployment. Twenty-five NL prompts addressing cohort identification and characterization in an adult ICD-10 C71-coded brain-tumor cohort (n = 1,594) were evaluated against manually written reference SQL and checked for a corresponding executed query in the exported log. Responses were classified into five categories. Prompts with unanswered or incorrect responses were re-posed in a new thread. Results: The platform was implemented over two years. Fifteen of 25 responses were exact (n = 11), concordant after definition alignment (n = 1), or incorrect but traceable from the logged SQL (n = 3); six were plausible but incorrect without a logged query, and four remained unanswered. No incorrect unlogged result recurred in a new thread. Across the initial and repeat evaluations, 22 of 23 logged responses were correct or traceable, whereas all eight unlogged responses were incorrect. Conclusions: Implementation was feasible but required substantial local institutional preparation. The NL interface reproduced SQL-derived results when definitions were explicit, while query-level provenance and verification of the displayed result were critical for identifying unreliable outputs.

title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
desc: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

title: Beyond the Stethoscope: Artificial Intelligence for Heart Failure Diagnosis and Phenotyping.
desc: [Journal of cardiac failure] Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping cardiovascular medicine by transforming routinely collected clinical data into tools for earlier disease detection and more precise phenotyping. Heart failure (HF) represents a particularly compelling opportunity for AI-driven innovation, as many patients with structural heart disease remain unrecognized and traditional diagnostic frameworks often fail to capture disease heterogeneity. AI-enabled electrocardiogram (ECG) models, including EchoNext and PRESENT-SHD, highlight the potential for scalable opportunistic screening strategies for structural heart disease. Multimodal approaches, using ECGs and echocardiograms, are enabling earlier recognition of specific HF phenotypes, such as transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. Successful implementation of these technologies will require prospective evaluation, thoughtful workflow integration, and responsible deployment. Early-career cardiologists are uniquely positioned to lead this transformation of AI in clinical medicine, ensuring that AI serves as a tool to augment clinical reasoning and ultimately advances more personalized, patient-centered cardiovascular care.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Imaging for Diagnosis and Management of Focal Liver Lesions
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Sun Yat-sen University; conditions: Focal Liver Lesions; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 10000; status: RECRUITING] This study aims to evaluate the clinical value of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted medical imaging in the diagnosis and management of focal liver lesions. Accurate diagnosis of focal liver lesions is important for selecting appropriate treatment strategies. However, distinguishing between different types of liver lesions can be challenging because of overlapping imaging features. AI-based imaging systems may help improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making.

title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
desc: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

title: Opinion: AI’s health advice can be accurate and still make us sicker
desc: Accurate public health campaign messages can fail or even backfire. The problem may be particularly acute with AI and medicine.
